label: A
title: A Class Visit to an Earth Science Centre
paragraphs: Our class visited a small Earth science centre near the sea. Our guide, Anna, welcomed us and invited us to ask questions. Nobody seemed afraid of giving a wrong answer. The friendly `atmosphere` helped us relax.

Before going inside, we stopped at a large window. We could see the `horizon`, where the sea seemed to meet the sky. Anna showed us a map with the centre's `longitude` and `latitude`. These two numbers helped us find its position. Its `altitude` was also marked: it stood twenty metres above sea level.

The map showed where we were on Earth. A model in the next room helped us look beneath its surface. Anna pointed to the `crust`, its thin outer layer, and the `mantle` below it. The crust and the hard upper part of the mantle together form the `lithosphere`. Blue areas on another model represented the `hydrosphere`: all the water on Earth, including water in rivers, seas and ice.

Some rusty nails beside the models showed how water and air could change everyday objects. We learned that iron can react with `oxygen` to form an `oxide`. Anna used this example to explain that chemical reactions can join substances together or break them apart. She then showed us a short film in which scientists split water to get `hydrogen`. Water was also part of the next example, which showed how plants use it, sunlight and `carbon dioxide` to grow.

As well as explaining how nature works, the centre showed what happens when it threatens people's lives. One room told the story of a town hit by a flood. The `disaster` had destroyed houses and roads. Its effects were `catastrophic`: many families lost both their homes and their farms. An old newspaper called it 'a `calamity` for the whole town'. Photos showed neighbours helping one another rebuild.

Our own visit had only one `mishap`: I dropped my notebook in a puddle. A few pages got wet, but my notes were still readable. Before we left, Anna explained why a path outside was closed. Loose rocks could `endanger` visitors. The centre would not `jeopardise` anyone's safety for a better view. Keeping people safe was at the `core` of its work.

occurrences.note: 本文指参观时友好、轻松的气氛。
本篇沿用已选定的“地壳”义。
岩石圈包括地壳和地幔最上部的坚硬部分。
本文指安全在这项工作中的核心地位。

label: B
title: A Rainy Weekend at Grandad's Farm
paragraphs: I had planned to help Grandad in his `greenhouse`, where he grew tomatoes under glass. But just as we reached the door, a sudden `gust` blew a bucket across the yard. The gentle `breeze` we had enjoyed at breakfast was gone. Grandad checked the weather report and decided that the plants could wait.

Indoors, the television showed farms damaged by violent weather. Grandad called such storms `destructive` because they could ruin months of hard work in a single night. The presenter also mentioned `El Niño`. She explained that this weather `phenomenon` began with warmer water in part of the Pacific Ocean and could affect weather far away.

That was something Grandad understood from experience. He had worked on farms in several countries when he was young. During the summer `monsoon` in India, the seasonal winds brought weeks of rain. In another year, a `typhoon` forced him to stay indoors in the Philippines. He showed me a photograph of a fallen tree outside his room.

I asked whether a `hurricane` was a different kind of storm. Grandad explained that hurricanes and typhoons were the same type of powerful tropical storm, named differently in different regions. A `tornado`, however, had a much narrower, spinning column of air reaching down to the ground. He drew its shape on an envelope. Looking at the pictures, I was glad we only had a `gale` outside, although even that strong wind made the windows shake.

With no chance of working outdoors, Grandad suggested looking through his old stone collection. I picked up a smooth `pebble` from a beach. He placed a `magnet` near a different sample, and it pulled the sample towards it. The dark piece was iron `ore`, rock from which people could obtain iron. That started a conversation about what rocks were made of. Grandad showed me a clear piece of `quartz`, a `mineral` found in many rocks. We could even see small pieces of it in a block of `granite`.

Beside the collection was a white `marble` bowl that he had bought on his travels. It held a photograph taken near a `volcano`. I asked if he had seen it `erupt`. 'Fortunately, no,' he said. 'The ground was quiet while I was there.' By then the wind outside was quieter too. We made some tea and agreed to check the tomatoes in the morning.

occurrences.note: 专名；本文按厄尔尼诺现象理解。

label: C
title: Choosing a Safer Place for a Youth Camp
paragraphs: Our town wanted to reopen a youth camp after years of closure. Before choosing a site, the organisers invited a scientist, Dr Lee, to speak to local families. Some people were annoyed by the delay. One father began to `fume` when he heard that another inspection was needed. Dr Lee stayed calm and explained why a cheap, attractive site was not always a safe one.

She began with the old camp beside the river. It had a beautiful `landscape`, with trees and water visible from every window. But the surrounding `terrain` was low and difficult to cross after rain. The river spread into several channels near its mouth, forming a `delta`. A nearby `swamp` stayed wet throughout the year. These features helped explain why `flooding` had repeatedly closed the access road.

A video showed the river during a heavy storm. A quiet stretch of water had become a `torrent`, carrying branches past the camp. Dr Lee then showed a photograph taken during a `drought`. The same river was nearly dry after months without enough rain. Neither picture told the whole story by itself. The organisers needed records from several years.

The other possible site was farther inland, beneath a rocky `cliff` with a small `cave` at its foot. It was higher, but Dr Lee wanted the rock checked before anyone slept below it. She compared this with work she had done elsewhere. On another `continent`, her team had studied a mountain camp below a `glacier`. An `avalanche` there had sent snow down towards an empty building. A good view had almost hidden a serious risk.

Her wider research also helped her judge local risks. Near a volcano, `seismic` instruments could record shaking caused by an `earthquake` or movement underground. Other researchers used a `thermodynamic` model to study heat and pressure in `magma`. Coastal teams watched for a `tsunami` after powerful earthquakes beneath the sea. She explained that different places needed different checks; our inland camp did not face every danger in her photographs.

Air quality mattered too. Morning `mist` was usually just tiny drops of water hanging in the air. Traffic-related `smog` was a different concern, especially beside a busy road. By the end, the angry father was asking practical questions. The families agreed to wait for the inspections before voting. They wanted a camp their children could enjoy safely for years.

occurrences.note: begin to fume：开始发怒。本文学习的是动词。
thermodynamic model：研究热、能量等关系的热力学模型。

label: D
title: Helping a Traveller Tell Her Story
paragraphs: When our library invited Maya to give a talk about her travels, I offered to help with the display. She arrived in a `plain` blue shirt with no pattern or decoration. Instead of bringing an expensive screen, she carried a box of photographs and an old `globe`.

As we turned the model, Maya traced a journey across the `equator` from the northern `hemisphere` to the southern one. The globe spun around a metal `axis`. Following her route on it helped me put the photographs in order.

Her first picture showed a trip on a local river. She was pushing a long wooden `pole` against the riverbed to move a small boat forward. Her later journeys had taken her much farther: across the `Atlantic` and into the `Mediterranean`. After weeks on the `ocean`, she had continued inland. One photograph showed a village on a high `plateau`. In another, travellers rested beside an `oasis`, where water allowed trees to grow in otherwise dry surroundings. We could see how the land changed along her route.

Her later journeys took her much farther from those warm places. She had visited an `Arctic` research station and travelled with an `Antarctic` team. Comparing the two sets of pictures helped us understand why scientists study both `polar` regions. The people in the photographs were doing ordinary jobs as well as research: cooking meals, repairing doors and checking supplies.

However, Maya did not want the display to be only about beautiful places. At one site, the weather had started to `deteriorate` while her team was working. Stronger winds would `aggravate` their problems, so they returned early. At another site, heavy vehicles could `degrade` the ground, making it less able to support plants. Once plants were lost, wind and rain could `erode` the exposed soil. The team had asked for money to `upgrade` an old path so that vehicles could stay on one route.

These decisions were part of a longer tradition of careful travel. Maya ended with a page from an old explorer's diary. 'Our intentions are entirely `pacific`,' he had written before meeting a local community. Maya explained that he meant peaceful: he wanted to learn, not fight. It was a formal word, but a simple idea. We placed the diary beside her photographs of shared meals and local guides.

occurrences.note: 本文指无图案、无装饰的朴素衬衫。
本文修饰 research station，指北极地区的研究站；正文按地理名称惯例写 Arctic。
本文修饰 team，指在南极活动的团队。
本文指车辆使土地退化，土地更难支持植物生长。
较正式；本文放在故事中的旧日记引文里，指和平的意图。

label: E
title: Checking a Coastal Walking Route
paragraphs: Our walking club wanted to publish a guide to the paths around a small `gulf`. Before printing it, we asked a `marine` scientist, Eva, to join us for a day. She studied animals living in the sea and knew this part of the `coast` well. We also brought the `current` map, because several paths had changed since the old one was printed.

At first, the walk seemed easy. A `flat` path crossed the grass behind a wide `beach`. The `sandy` ground near the water was soft under our shoes, but farther along it became `stony`. Some rocks were `smooth` from years in the water. Others had a `rough` surface that felt sharp against my hand. We noted where people might need stronger shoes.

The route then left the sea and followed a little `brook` through the trees. It joined a larger `stream` near an old bridge. The water here was `shallow`, and we could see the bottom clearly. A few empty bottles lay beside it. We picked them up, but Eva asked us to think beyond the rubbish we could see. The `source` of the plastic might be a picnic area farther upstream. Cleaning one spot would not solve the problem if more bottles kept arriving.

I realised that my understanding of the area had been rather `superficial`. I had looked at views without asking how the water, paths and people affected one another. Eva suggested adding a little of this information to our guide. Readers could enjoy the walk and understand why keeping the streams clean mattered to the sea as well.

Back on the `shore`, we checked a path beneath an almost `vertical` rock wall. A `steep` set of steps led to higher ground. The map showed another route across the sand, but Eva warned us to check the `tide`. Water could cover that route later in the day, leaving walkers cut off. Accurate `navigation` meant more than knowing which direction to take. We also needed to know when a path was safe.

We chose the steps and reached the top before lunch. From there, we could see the whole route we had walked. Our guide would still mention the lovely views, but it would also show the difficult surfaces, the safe way uphill and the need to check sea conditions. That would make it useful to someone visiting for the first time.

occurrences.note: 本文指当前使用的地图。
本文指对当地环境的理解肤浅。

label: F
title: Getting Ready to Visit Lucy
paragraphs: My cousin Lucy had moved to Australia and invited me to visit. I found her town on a map of `Oceania`, then looked more closely at the local streets. Her home was on a `peninsula` reaching out from the `mainland`, with water on three sides. Two `parallel` roads ran towards its end. Lucy marked the correct one for me and warned that her own street was too `narrow` for a large car to turn around easily.

Once I knew how to get there, I asked what clothes to bring. Lucy said the `climate` was generally `mild`, with winters much less cold than those I knew. However, the `weather` could change during a single afternoon. Her message made me curious, so I read a short article about `meteorology`, the study of weather. It helped me understand why a local forecast was more useful for packing than a yearly average.

I also noticed that her town lay just south of a `tropic`, the Tropic of Capricorn. I had imagined that every place near that line would be dry. Lucy corrected me. Some inland areas were `arid`, but the air around her coastal home could be very `humid`. Even a day without rain could feel uncomfortable because there was so much moisture in the air.

Living there had made Lucy pay more attention to her house. On `warm` days, she opened windows on opposite sides to let air move through. When the air outside was dry enough, this also helped dry her clothes. Otherwise, they could stay `damp` for hours. She was more careful with the plants beside the window: their soil needed to remain `moist`, so she checked it before adding water.

In winter, she used `heating`, but she tried to keep it at a `moderate` level rather than turn every room into a hot box. She had recently asked a builder how well the house kept heat inside in winter and outside in summer. His report called this its `thermal` performance. Better windows, he said, could make it more comfortable without using so much electricity.

Her photographs looked very different from the view outside my own window. It had been a `snowy` morning at home, with snow falling steadily outside. The previous day, a thin layer of white `frost` had covered the garden before the sun came up. I crossed my heavy coat off the packing list and added a light rain jacket instead.

occurrences.note: 本文的 a tropic 指一条回归线，后文具体说南回归线。
本文修饰空气，表示空气中水分多。
thermal performance：房屋在保留和阻隔热量方面的表现。
本文指当时正在下雪的早晨。

label: G
title: A Walk That Ended Early
paragraphs: My brother and I had waited a week for our walk. The previous weekend had been `frigid`, with air so cold that we stayed indoors. This Saturday looked better. The weather `forecast` showed a dry morning, although it warned that the afternoon might turn `stormy`. We agreed to leave early and return before lunch.

At the park gate, the `temperature` was only four degrees `Celsius`. Water could still `freeze` overnight, and a little ice remained beside the path. We expected it to `thaw` when the sun reached it. Even with the sunshine, there was a `chill` in the air. I pulled up my collar and began to `shiver` while my brother checked the route. His hands seemed to `tremble` too, so we decided to keep moving.

For an hour, everything went well. Then the clouds became much darker. Small balls of `hail` struck the path, and we turned back. A flash of `lightning` appeared beyond the trees. A few seconds later, we heard `thunder`. We were still some distance from the gate, and my worries began to `mount` as the sky grew darker.

We followed the shortest route to the visitor centre, where other walkers were taking shelter. By the time we reached the door, the rain had become a `downpour`. Water poured from the roof into the yard. Inside, a display showed the total `rainfall` for the month. After several wet days, the figure was already above the usual monthly total. Looking outside, I could see why.

The storm reached its `peak` around noon, when the rain was heaviest and we could hardly hear one another speak. Then the noise slowly faded. Later, sunlight appeared through the clouds, and a `rainbow` stretched across the wet fields. We waited until the staff said it was safe to leave, then caught a bus home rather than continue the walk.

I changed out of my wet clothes and had a hot `shower`. My brother made soup while I warmed up. When it was ready, he asked me to `sprinkle` a little salt into my bowl. We ate beside the window and watched the last clouds move away. The walk had been short, but neither of us felt that we had missed out. Getting home safely was enough for one day.

occurrences.note: four degrees Celsius：摄氏四度。
本文是动词，指结成的冰融化。
worries begin to mount：担忧逐渐增加。
total rainfall：累计降雨量。
本文指暴风雨强度达到的最高点。
have a hot shower：洗个热水澡；本文 shower 为名词。

label: H
title: Planning Changes to an Old Garden
paragraphs: Our village stood in a `valley` below a high `mountain`. For years, an old public garden on the `hillside` had been nearly empty. Its owner, the local council, invited residents to suggest improvements. I joined a small group that walked around the site before drawing up a plan.

A map at the gate showed where everything was. The entrance was in the `southwest`, while a small pond lay in the `southeast`. From the entrance, a path crossed the `southern` part of the garden. It climbed a gentle `slope` before reaching a long `ridge`, where a seat offered a view of the village. The climb was manageable for us, but we knew that some older visitors would need places to rest.

We continued towards the `northeast` to inspect the oldest part of the garden. A shelter stood against the `eastern` wall. An old guidebook described it as an '`oriental` pavilion', a broad label for its East Asian design. For the new guide, we agreed to explain the design more precisely once we had checked its history. Repeating the old label would tell visitors very little.

The ground nearby needed attention as well. Stones lay `irregularly` along the path, with no even pattern or spacing. This made the surface difficult for wheelchairs. Simply covering it with loose stones would be `inappropriate`, so we asked an adviser about a firmer surface. The council gave us a budget in the `range` of five to six thousand pounds. We could not repair everything, but we did not want to `overlook` visitors who could not use the current path.

In the `northwest`, we found another problem. Water from an `abnormal` period of heavy rain had carried soil into the pond. A thick layer of `sediment` had settled on the bottom. Some work was `inevitable`: leaving it alone would mean losing much of the open water. However, removing every tree nearby would cause `irreversible` damage to the old garden. Once its oldest trees were gone, that part of the garden's history would be lost forever.

Our final plan kept the healthy trees, improved the main path and called for careful cleaning of the pond. It was smaller than some residents had hoped, but each change answered a problem we had actually seen. We included photographs and a clear map so that everyone at the next meeting could understand the choices.

occurrences.meaning: 东方的；东亚的（旧称，慎用）
occurrences.note: 旧称，慎用。本文引用旧导览册对建筑设计的描述，随后说明要查明历史并写得更具体。
本文指石头排列不规则，间距不均。
in the range of five to six thousand pounds：在五千至六千英镑的范围内。
本文指忽略无法使用现有道路的访客。

label: I
title: A Village Checks Its River
paragraphs: I grew up in a `suburb`, but my aunt lived in a small `rural` community farther up the river. Her village was on the `fringe` of a large area of farmland. Last spring, she asked me to come to a meeting about the river. A new factory was planned just beyond the village `border`, on land `adjacent` to the water.

The company had considered a site on the `outskirts` of the nearest city, but the village land was cheaper. Residents wanted jobs, yet they also depended on the river for their fields. They worried that `toxic` waste might enter the water. A scientist invited to the meeting explained that `pollution` could travel far beyond the place where it began. A chemical `pollutant` released upstream might `contaminate` water used by other communities.

To judge the risk, the village needed more than rumours. A teacher whose subject was `geology` offered to help collect samples. She explained that different types of ground could affect how water moved. Beside the river, thick `clay` held water after rain. Along the slower stretches, fine `silt` settled on the bottom. We would take samples from several places and have them tested.

My aunt and I joined the first trip. The riverbank was `muddy`, and I nearly lost a shoe. We also visited a `remote` bend that had no road leading to it. From there, the factory site looked `distant`, although it was only a few kilometres downstream. An empty building stood on the opposite bank, surrounded by broken fencing. The place felt `desolate`, with no people or signs of recent use.

Back at my aunt's house, I noticed `dirt` on my hands and under my nails. I washed carefully before touching any food. My aunt put a `plate` of sandwiches on the table while I wrote up our notes. The samples looked ordinary, but we knew that looking at water could not prove it was clean. We waited for the laboratory results before drawing conclusions.

The meeting a month later ended with a vote. Residents supported the factory only if the company accepted regular independent water tests. The proposal passed by a `margin` of six votes: twenty-eight in favour and twenty-two against. My aunt was pleased, but she kept the sampling notes. An agreement was useful only if people checked that it was being followed.

occurrences.note: 词条本身就是复数：on the outskirts of a city（在一座城市的郊区）。
a plate of sandwiches：一盘三明治。
本文的六票差额，来自二十八票与二十二票之差。

label: J
title: Making a Garden from an Empty Yard
paragraphs: When a small workshop closed, our neighbourhood was left with an empty yard. Broken roof tiles and other `debris` covered the ground. A long `crack` ran down one wall. Some residents imagined a `grand` entrance with stone steps, but most of us wanted somewhere to sit and grow plants. There was a clear `gap` between the money available and the cost of the more ambitious designs.

At our first meeting, Sara showed pictures from a recent camping trip. One photograph captured a `magnificent` view across a `desert` at evening. She had enjoyed the open `wilderness`, far from roads and buildings. However, the yard could not become a copy of that landscape. We needed shade in summer, food for insects and plants that would grow in our local weather.

Her photographs still gave us an `interesting` idea: make visitors notice how different kinds of ground support different plants. An old vegetable patch next door had dark, `fertile` soil, while the yard looked almost `barren`, with very little growing in it. A gardener tested the soil and showed us how to improve it. We would also need to `fertilise` the new vegetable beds, adding nutrients as the crops grew.

We wanted to keep the two mature trees by the wall. Sara explained that, when people `deforest` land by clearing its trees, the result can be much more serious than a less attractive view. Wildlife loses shelter, and exposed soil is more easily washed away. Our little project would work with the trees already there. Their shade would also make the seats more comfortable.

An electrician helped us choose `solar` lights that used energy from the sun. They lit the paths without making the whole garden too bright. That suited our astronomy club, which planned to meet there to watch a `lunar` eclipse. They hoped to see Earth's shadow move across the Moon. We marked the date on a `calendar` in the tool shed and left a clear space for their equipment.

In just a few weeks, there had been a `dramatic` increase in the amount of green space, from two small patches to most of the yard. 'You've done a `splendid` job,' an elderly neighbour told us on opening day. A child gave a shorter opinion: 'It's `super`!' Sara arrived at `sunrise` to take a photograph before anyone disturbed the paths. At `sunset`, we sat under the trees and looked at the same view. The yard finally felt like part of the neighbourhood again.

occurrences.note: 本文指可用资金与较高设计费用之间的差距。
本文指给菜地施肥、补充养分。
deforest land：砍去某片土地上的森林。本文谈的是毁林带来的影响。
本文 solar lights 指太阳能灯。
lunar eclipse：月食；lunar 修饰 eclipse，表示与月球有关。
本文指短期内绿地面积急剧增加。
